There is something odd in your syntax--the line
psychological involvement~~0*psychological involvement
says that this factor has a variance of 0, which would mean that it cannot be a predictor of anything. (If this factor was a dependent variable, then the line would refer to its residual variance, but I don't see this factor being dependent on anything. In addition, allowing the loading for this factor's first indicator to equal 1 says something different and probably incompatible about this factor's variance. I would start by deleting the line of code that forces the factor variance to 0.
     Some of your group sample sizes are very, very small. With only 40 or so observations per group, nonconvergence is a real possibility, unless the model fits very, very well and you provide good starting values. Across-group constraints would help, if they are consistent with the data.

On Tuesday, September 6, 2016 at 10:30:04 PM UTC-4, Edward Rigdon wrote:

There is something odd in your syntax--the line
psychological involvement~~0*psychological involvement
says that this factor has a variance of 0, which would mean that it cannot be a predictor of anything. (If this factor was a dependent variable, then the line would refer to its residual variance, but I don't see this factor being dependent on anything. In addition, allowing the loading for this factor's first indicator to equal 1 says something different and probably incompatible about this factor's variance. I would start by deleting the line of code that forces the factor variance to 0.
     Some of your group sample sizes are very, very small. With only 40 or so observations per group, nonconvergence is a real possibility, unless the model fits very, very well and you provide good starting values. Across-group constraints would help, if they are consistent with the data.

messages.subject: Re: convergence problem
parts:
I constrained the variance of this factor "psychological involvement" to 0, because If there is no such constraint, the following problem would occur:  lavaan WARNING: could not compute standard errors!

Strange that you see that warning, yet the output does contain standard errors.  Is this warning only occurring when you constrain the variance to zero?

Regarding the other warnings, it is not recommended to constrain parameters to zero just to prevent estimates beyond the boundary.  What does your correlation matrix look like between those 3 variables (SP.Psy1-3)?  The loadings are high, but such a low (especially negative) exogenous common-factor variance indicates the variables don't actually have a common cause, at least not one that explains a substantial amount of their (co)variances.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

I didn't ask about the correlations among latent variables.  That covariance matrix can't be (fully) converted to correlation because you can't take the square root of a negative variance to get the SD.

I asked about the observed correlation matrix for the three indicators of the construct that has negative variance.
